title: Your Work Style

intake.question: Where are you with work right now?
What drains you most at work?

options.label: Boredom, the same thing every day

plan.title: What your elements do at work
How you burn out, and how you come back
Feedback: taking it and giving it
The job vibe that fits you

strong.text: Your chart is strong, so this style comes at full intensity. You can work long and hard without external motivation, and you trust your process. The risk is that you set the pace for everyone around you without noticing. Check in with colleagues on timelines rather than assuming they'll keep up. Being fast is a strength; being the only one who knows the plan is a bottleneck.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Share the plan out loud. Speed alone makes you a bottleneck.

weak.text: Your chart is the lighter kind, so this style shows up best when you feel supported. In the right team you're quietly excellent; in a hostile one you second-guess yourself. Choose environments carefully, and keep a record of your wins. Weak charts often forget their successes and remember every mistake, which skews how you see your own work.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Keep a wins file. Your memory only saves the mistakes.

strong.text: With a strong chart you lead naturally, sometimes before anyone asked you to. People follow your confidence. The note is about space: strong leaders can fill every silence with their own ideas. Try ending meetings with 'What am I missing?' and wait through the awkward pause. The best idea in the room often arrives after second seven.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: 'What am I missing?' Then wait through the awkward pause.

weak.text: With a weak chart you may not see yourself as a leader at all, and yet people come to you. You lead by example, attention and care. Claim it. Ask for the title when the work is already yours. Leadership that comes from service is just as real as leadership that comes from command, and often lasts longer.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: People already follow you. Ask for the title that matches.

strong.text: Strong charts can dominate a team without meaning to. You talk first, decide fast and move on, while quieter colleagues are still processing. Make room deliberately: ask the quiet person's opinion by name, and give people time to disagree with you in writing. You'll get better ideas and fewer silent grudges.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ask the quiet colleague by name. Their idea might be the one.

weak.text: Weak charts at work often become the team's peacekeeper and its dumping ground. You're easy to ask, so people ask. Practice saying 'Let me check my week first' before agreeing to anything. It isn't rude. It's how people learn your time has value.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: 'Let me check my week first.' Say it before every yes.

strong.text: Strong charts burn out late and hard, because you can push through the early warnings for months. You might not believe you're burning out until your body or your temper insists. Schedule recovery like a meeting. Treat a holiday as part of the job, not a reward you earn when the job is done, because the job is never done.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Vacation goes in the calendar first. Work fits around it.

weak.text: Weak charts burn out earlier and more often, but you also notice it sooner, which is an advantage. Act on the first signs instead of waiting to be sure. One quiet day at the first wave of exhaustion saves you three weeks later. Your sensitivity is an early warning system. Trust it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your sensitivity is an alarm. Answer it on the first ring.

strong.text: With a strong chart, you'll do best in roles with real authority and real challenge. Too much hand-holding feels like a cage. Look for jobs where you own outcomes, have a say in strategy, and can see your impact. Then pick a team that will tell you honestly when you're steamrolling.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Own outcomes, and keep one colleague who'll tell you the truth.

weak.text: With a weak chart, the culture matters as much as the role. A great job in a harsh workplace will drain you; a modest job with kind, competent people will let you grow fast. Ask in interviews how the team handles mistakes. The answer tells you more than the job description.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ask how they handle mistakes. That's the real job description.

peer_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {dm_el}, your own element, the peer family: colleagues, competitors, partners. At work this makes you independent and competitive. You measure yourself against your peers, you want equal treatment and credit, and you work brilliantly in partnerships of equals. You can resist taking direction from people you don't respect. The gift is self-reliance. The work is collaboration: sharing credit generously and letting others lead sometimes without seeing it as losing.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Peer-heavy: you'd rather have a rival than a boss. Share the credit anyway.

output_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces, the output family: creativity, expression, skill. At work you're the ideas person, the maker, the one with a talent people notice. You chafe at rules and bureaucracy and do your best work when you're trusted to create. The shadow is criticizing authority a little too openly. Channel it into building better systems rather than mocking the existing ones.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Output-heavy: the maker. Build better systems instead of mocking the old ones.

wealth_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls, the wealth family: resources, results, management. At work you think in outcomes. You're good with budgets, logistics and turning plans into deliverables, and you like being measured on what you achieve. The shadow is treating people like resources. Remember that the spreadsheet has humans in it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Wealth-heavy: results matter, and so do the people producing them.

power_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that controls your {dm_el}, the power family: authority, structure, responsibility. On a strong chart this is the natural manager pattern. You understand hierarchy, respect rules, and can carry serious responsibility. The shadow is rigidity and taking work so seriously that you forget to enjoy it. Leave some room for the unexpected.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Power-heavy: born manager. Leave some room for fun at work.

resource_strong.text: Your chart is heavy on {heavy_el}, the element that feeds your {dm_el}, the resource family: knowledge, learning, support. At work you're the expert, the researcher, the person who understands the theory behind everything. You can get stuck in analysis and wait too long to act. Ship the draft. Your knowledge is worth most when it reaches people.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Resource-heavy: the expert. Ship the draft before it's perfect.

output_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} produces: effort, expression, output. On a weak chart this is the overworker pattern. You produce a lot, help everyone and pour yourself into your work until you're empty. Your talent is real. Your energy is finite. Measure your work by impact, not hours, and stop when the important part is done.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Measure impact, not hours. Stop when the important part's done.

wealth_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element your {dm_el} controls, the pattern classical readers call wealth heavy, self light: a lot to manage, not much backup. At work you can end up responsible for more than your role or your energy can hold, budgets, people, other teams' problems. Ask for resources before you accept responsibility. 'I can take that on if I get help with X' is a professional sentence.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ask for resources before you say yes. That's not weakness.

power_weak.text: Your chart leans on {heavy_el}, the element that presses on your {dm_el}: pressure, authority, rules. On a weak chart this can feel like working under a constant inspection. You're conscientious and reliable, and criticism from bosses lands heavily. Find managers who are clear and kind, and keep proof of your good work for the days the inner critic gets loud.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Clear, kind managers. Look for them on purpose.

rooted_on_paper.text: At work this looks like someone who seems confident in meetings and then rereads their own emails three times afterward. Colleagues think you've got it handled. Some days you do; some days you're running on willpower. Both are real. Choose roles where support is built in, a good manager, a strong team, and stop expecting yourself to look fine every day.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Confident in the meeting, rereading the email three times after.

output_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the output element, how work becomes visible. A strong chart without output can do great work that nobody sees. You get it done and move on without telling anyone. Borrow some output: a short weekly update, a demo, a sentence in the team meeting about what you finished.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Great work nobody sees doesn't count at reviews. Send the update.

wealth_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the wealth element, the pull toward measurable results. You're capable and confident but may care more about the work itself than where it leads. That's lovely until reviews come around. Set one concrete target per quarter that you can point to.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: One concrete target per quarter. Something you can point at.

power_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the power element, structure and authority. A strong chart without power resists being managed and may struggle in hierarchies. Build your own structure instead: deadlines you set yourself, a mentor you chose, rules you'd actually follow.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: No structure built in? Build your own. Deadlines you chose.

resource_strong.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the resource element, learning and support. You push forward on talent and drive and rarely stop to learn or ask for help. Schedule learning like a meeting: a course, a mentor, a book a month. It compounds.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: A book a month, a mentor, a course. Talent needs feeding.

output_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the output element, expression. That protects a weak chart from overworking. It can also keep your ideas inside your head. Share one idea per week, in writing, with your name on it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your ideas deserve daylight. Sign them.

wealth_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the wealth element, the urge to chase results. You don't push for the promotion, the project or the raise, which keeps you calm and keeps you overlooked. Ask for one thing per year, clearly and in advance.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ask for one thing a year. Clearly. In advance.

power_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the power element, outside pressure. Fewer rules weighing on you, which is good for your nerves. You may need help with structure: a clear role, written priorities, a manager who sets expectations explicitly.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ask for written priorities. Clarity is kindness for you.

resource_weak.text: {miss_el} is missing from your visible chart, and for your {dm_el} it's the resource element, support and learning. You work on willpower without much backup. Build your support on purpose: one mentor, one colleague you trust, one learning habit that refills you instead of draining you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: One mentor, one trusted colleague, one habit that refills you.

none_strong.text: All five elements turn up in your pillars. For a strong chart that's range: you can manage, create, analyze and lead. The trap is being good at everything and known for nothing. Pick the one skill you want people to name when they describe you, and sharpen it on purpose.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Good at everything, known for nothing? Pick your one skill.

none_weak.text: All five elements turn up in your pillars. For a weak chart that's flexibility: you can fit almost any team or role. Don't let flexible turn into overlooked. Choose the work you want more of and say so, out loud, to the person who assigns it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Tell whoever assigns the work what you'd like more of.

resource.title: What refills you at work: {helper_el}
resource.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. For your weak {dm_el} chart it's {helper_el}, the element that feeds your Day Master. At work that means mentors, learning, supportive managers and real rest. You do your best work after you've been taught and looked after, so choose roles where that's part of the culture, not a perk.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your refill element is {helper_el}: mentors, learning, real rest.

peer.title: What steadies you at work: {helper_el}, your own element
peer.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. Yours already has plenty of nourishment on paper, so what steadies you is your own element, {helper_el}. At work that means peers: a work friend, a partner on projects, colleagues at your level you can be honest with. Find your people at work, they're your best resource.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your steadying element is {helper_el}: a real work friend.

output.title: Where your extra drive should go: {helper_el}
output.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. A strong {dm_el} chart needs an outlet, and yours is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master produces. At work that means making things: building, writing, designing, teaching. Energy without output turns into micromanagement and office politics.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your outlet is {helper_el}. Make things, or you'll start managing people too hard.

wealth.title: What balances you at work: {helper_el}
wealth.text: Every chart has an element that brings it back to balance. Yours is strong and already expressive, so what balances you is {helper_el}, the element your Day Master shapes. At work that means concrete goals and measurable results: a target, a budget, a launch date. Aim your energy at something you can finish.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your balance is {helper_el}: a goal you can actually finish.

wood.text: Wood at work: growth plans, learning a new skill each year, mentoring someone, and a desk near a window or plants.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood for you: a growth plan, a mentee, a plant on the desk.

fire.text: Fire at work: visibility, presenting your work, energetic teammates, celebrating wins, and natural light.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Fire for you: present your work, celebrate wins, sit in the light.

earth.text: Earth at work: routine, a stable team, a clear role, regular lunch breaks and a workspace that feels like yours.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth for you: routine, real lunch breaks, a desk that's yours.

metal.text: Metal at work: clear priorities, tidy systems, saying no to low-value tasks, and finishing things completely.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal for you: clear priorities and saying no to the fluff.

water.text: Water at work: thinking time, flexible hours, research, travel, quiet spaces and room to explore ideas.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water for you: thinking time, flexibility, a quiet corner.

rat.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Rat, 子, midnight Water: resourceful, quick and observant. You quietly know who really makes decisions in the office and how to get things done through side doors.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rat underneath: you know who really decides things. Quietly.

ox.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Ox, 丑, cold wet Earth: patient, enduring and stubborn. You'll outlast every reorganization and still be doing excellent work when the flashy hires have left.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ox underneath: you outlast every reorg. Every single one.

tiger.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Tiger, 寅, early spring Wood: bold, restless and protective. You'll volunteer for the scary project and defend your team against unfair treatment.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Tiger underneath: first hand up for the scary project.

rabbit.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Rabbit, 卯, spring Wood: diplomatic, tasteful and conflict-averse. You make the office nicer, and you'd do almost anything to avoid an open argument.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Rabbit underneath: you'd write a novel to avoid one argument.

dragon.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Dragon, 辰, damp Earth storing Water: ambitious, imaginative and more complex than your work persona shows. You think in big plans and keep some of them very private.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Dragon underneath: big private plans, shared on a need-to-know basis.

snake.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Snake, 巳, early summer Fire: strategic, perceptive and discreet. You read office politics like a novel and rarely reveal your next move.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Snake underneath: you see three moves ahead in every meeting.

horse.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Horse, 午, midsummer Fire: energetic, independent and impatient. You need freedom and movement at work, and a desk job with no variety makes you twitchy by noon.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Horse underneath: twitchy by noon at a desk with no variety.

goat.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Goat, 未, warm late-summer Earth: creative, kind and sensitive to atmosphere. A harsh office drains you, a gentle one lets your talent bloom.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Goat underneath: gentle offices make you bloom.

monkey.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Monkey, 申, early autumn Metal: clever, inventive and easily bored. You'll find a shortcut for any process and get restless if you can't use it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Monkey underneath: a shortcut for every process. Restless without one.

rooster.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Rooster, 酉, autumn Metal: precise, proud and detail-oriented. Your work is meticulous, and you notice when other people's isn't.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rooster underneath: meticulous, and you notice when others aren't.

dog.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Dog, 戌, dry autumn Earth: loyal, principled and protective. You'll stand up for a colleague being treated unfairly even when it costs you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Dog underneath: you'd defend a colleague even when it costs you.

pig.text: The branch under your Day Master shows the private you, the one close colleagues eventually meet. Yours is the Pig, 亥, early winter Water: generous, easygoing and honest. You share credit freely and assume good intentions, which makes you loved and occasionally taken advantage of.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Pig underneath: generous with credit. Keep a little for yourself.

day_branch_heading: Your day branch at work: the {day_animal} ({day_branch})

student.text: You're still studying, which means your work style is showing up in group projects, part-time jobs and how you study. That's useful data. Notice which group projects energize you and which ones you dread, because the same pattern will follow you into your first job. Try one internship or project in a field that matches the job vibe later in this reading, just to test it. And start a simple log of projects you loved. It becomes your first portfolio and your first honest map of what you're good at.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Group projects are data. Notice which ones light you up.

early.text: You're early in your career, the stage where you learn the most and have the least control. Use your work style knowingly: pick bosses who suit you more carefully than you pick companies. A great first manager teaches you more in a year than three courses. And keep a list of what you enjoy and what drains you; it'll guide your next move better than any salary table. Say yes to stretch tasks that teach you something, and no to ones that only teach you to be tired.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Pick the boss more carefully than the company. Seriously.

mid.text: You're a few years in, the stage where your strengths are visible and so are your habits. This is a good time to shape your role around what you do best instead of what you fell into. Talk to your manager about the parts of your job you'd like more of. People who ask for the right work at this stage tend to love their jobs five years later. This is also the stage to find a mentor two steps ahead of you. One lunch a quarter is plenty.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Shape the role around your strengths now. Ask for more of the good parts.

lead.text: You're leading people, which means your work style is now multiplied by everyone on your team. Your habits become their weather. Read the leadership chapter twice, then ask one person you trust what it's like to work for you. The answer will be more useful than any reading, including this one. And protect your own growth: leaders who stop learning start managing by habit.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your habits are now your team's weather. Ask what it's like.

between.text: You're between jobs, which is uncomfortable and also a rare moment to choose on purpose. Use the job vibe chapter as a filter, not a rulebook. Before your next interview, write down the three conditions you need to do your best work, the kind of team, pace and boss, and ask about each one. You're interviewing them too. Meanwhile, keep a daily rhythm. Structure between jobs keeps your confidence from leaking away.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Three conditions for your best work. Ask about each in interviews.

unsaid.text: You skipped the question about where you are, so this section is for anyone. Wherever you are, a student, mid-career, leading, between things, your work style shows up the same way: in what energizes you and what drains you. Keep both lists. They're more useful than any job title. Add a third list if you like: what you'd do even if nobody paid you. It often points somewhere useful.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Keep two lists: what energizes you, what drains you.

meetings.text: Endless meetings drain you. That usually means you need time to actually do the work, and talking about it feels like a tax. Protect two blocks of focus time a week in your calendar and treat them like client meetings. Ask for agendas, offer to answer by email, and leave meetings where you're not needed. Most people will admire it. If you run meetings yourself, cut them to twenty-five minutes. Everyone will love you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Two focus blocks a week. Guard them like client meetings.

unclear.text: Unclear goals drain you. You want to know what success looks like first; then you can really commit. Ask for it explicitly: 'What does done look like, and how will we know it worked?' If nobody can answer, write your own definition and send it around. People are usually relieved. Unclear goals also hide unclear priorities, so ask which two things matter most this month.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: 'What does done look like?' Ask it every time.

people.text: Difficult people drain you. That's universal, but for you it's the main cost of work, which says you care about the human side a lot. Pick one difficult person and change one thing about how you interact: the channel, the timing, the length. Small adjustments often fix more than big confrontations. And keep one ally in the building. A single friendly face changes how hard people feel.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Change one thing: channel, timing or length. Small fixes work.

boredom.text: Boredom drains you, the same thing every day. You need novelty and growth to stay engaged. Ask for one stretch project a year, learn something adjacent to your role, or redesign a boring process so it runs itself. Boredom is information: it means you've outgrown something. Until then, add variety at the edges: a new route to work, a different lunch spot, a side project.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Boredom means you've outgrown something. Ask for a stretch project.

unsaid.text: You didn't say what drains you, which is fair, because it changes week to week. Next time you feel exhausted after work, write down the one thing that took the most out of you. A month of notes will tell you more than this paragraph can. Patterns appear quickly once they're written down. Most people are surprised by what tops the list.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Write down what drained you most, every tired day for a month.

wood.heading: Your element at work: Wood
wood.text: Wood at work is growth and direction. Wood people need to feel they're developing, a new skill, a bigger scope, a project that's getting somewhere. Stagnation is the Wood nightmare: the same role for years with nothing to learn. You also tend to plan ahead and think in terms of where you'll be next year. Make sure your manager knows your growth goals, because Wood without a direction grows sideways, into frustration.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood needs growth. Tell your manager where you want to grow.

fire.heading: Your element at work: Fire
fire.text: Fire at work is visibility and energy. Fire people do their best work when it's seen and appreciated: presenting, pitching, leading the kickoff, celebrating the launch. You light up teams. Long invisible projects with no recognition dim you quickly. Ask for moments to show your work, and build in rest, because Fire burns brighter than it can sustain.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire needs an audience. Ask for chances to show your work.

earth.heading: Your element at work: Earth
earth.text: Earth at work is reliability and care. Earth people hold teams together, keep promises and build systems that last. You value stability and get uneasy with constant change. Your work is often underrated because it's steady rather than dramatic. Make your contribution visible, and when change comes, ask for the reasons. Earth adapts well once it understands why.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth adapts fine once it knows why. Ask for the reasons.

metal.heading: Your element at work: Metal
metal.text: Metal at work is precision and decisiveness. Metal people cut through noise, set standards and finish things. You like clear rules, clear goals and clear accountability. Vague cultures frustrate you. Your challenge is softness: delivering standards with warmth so people want to meet them rather than fear missing them.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal sets the bar. Deliver it warmly so people want to reach it.

water.heading: Your element at work: Water
water.text: Water at work is intelligence and adaptability. Water people see the big picture, connect ideas and navigate change easily. You need intellectual stimulation and some freedom in how you work. Rigid processes feel like a dam. Your challenge is focus: choosing where your current goes so it carves a canyon instead of spreading into a marsh.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water needs a channel. Pick where your current goes.

peer.heading: Your leadership tool
peer.text: With your own element the most common in your chart, your leadership tool is partnership. You lead best as first among equals: sharing decisions, building a team of strong peers, and treating people as colleagues rather than subordinates. Hire people who are better than you at something, and tell them so.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your tool is partnership. Hire people better than you at something.

output.heading: Your leadership tool
output.text: With your output element the most common in your chart, your leadership tool is inspiration. You lead by ideas, creativity and the way you talk about the work. People follow your vision. Pair it with someone who loves process, or the vision will stay a beautiful speech.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your tool is inspiration. Find a co-pilot who loves checklists.

wealth.heading: Your leadership tool
wealth.text: With your wealth element the most common in your chart, your leadership tool is execution. You lead by organizing resources, setting targets and getting results. Teams under you deliver. Make sure they also know why it matters; results feel better with a reason attached.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your tool is execution. Attach a reason to every target.

power.heading: Your leadership tool
power.text: With your power element the most common in your chart, your leadership tool is structure. You lead by clear roles, fair rules and accountability. People know where they stand. Add flexibility where it costs nothing; rules that bend for good reasons win more respect than rules that never bend.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Your tool is structure. Let rules bend when there's a good reason.

resource.heading: Your leadership tool
resource.text: With your resource element the most common in your chart, your leadership tool is mentoring. You lead by teaching, explaining and developing people. Your team learns a lot under you. Remember to decide too; teaching is not a substitute for making the call.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your tool is mentoring. Teaching doesn't replace making the call.

peer.heading: The coworker type you are
peer.text: As a coworker you're the equal: fair, independent, and quick to notice if credit or workload isn't split evenly. People trust you to be straight with them. Watch the competitive edge with colleagues at your level; most of them are on your side.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You count who did what. Most colleagues are on your side.

output.heading: The coworker type you are
output.text: As a coworker you're the creative spark: full of ideas, fun in brainstorms, and the person who makes the team chat entertaining. People enjoy you. Make sure your ideas come with an offer to help build them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: The brainstorm star. Stay for the building part too.

wealth.heading: The coworker type you are
wealth.text: As a coworker you're the organizer: the one with the shared tracker, the clear next steps and the reminder email. Teams run better with you. Sometimes people feel managed by a peer, so ask before you assign.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: The tracker person. Ask before assigning tasks to equals.

power.heading: The coworker type you are
power.text: As a coworker you're the reliable one: punctual, careful and true to your word. People bring you the important stuff. You can seem a little serious; a joke in the team chat now and then shows the human side.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Show the funny side now and then. People relax.

resource.heading: The coworker type you are
resource.text: As a coworker you're the expert and the listener: people ask you how things work and tell you how they feel. You're generous with both. Guard your own focus time, because being everyone's resource is a full-time job you didn't apply for.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Everyone's resource is a job you never applied for. Guard your time.

spring.heading: Your season of the work year
spring.text: Born in spring, your natural season at work is the start: new projects, new teams, the energy of the first quarter. You're at your best when something is beginning. Use the spring months for launches and big asks, and schedule the maintenance work for when your energy dips.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Spring-born: save your big asks for beginnings.

summer.heading: Your season of the work year
summer.text: Born in summer, your natural season at work is full speed: conferences, launches, busy periods when everything is happening at once. You thrive in intensity. Plan a real break right after your busiest stretch, because summer energy tends to crash in a heap.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Summer-born: book the break right after the busy season.

autumn.heading: Your season of the work year
autumn.text: Born in autumn, your natural season at work is review and harvest: closing projects, cleaning up processes, evaluating what worked. You're excellent at finishing. Make sure your finishing work is visible, because harvests are less glamorous than launches and just as important.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Autumn-born: make your finishing work visible.

winter.heading: Your season of the work year
winter.text: Born in winter, your natural season at work is planning and depth: research, strategy, quiet preparation before anyone else starts. You do your best thinking when things are calm. Protect the quiet weeks; they're where your best ideas come from.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Winter-born: the quiet weeks are where your best ideas live.

earth.heading: Your season of the work year
earth.text: Born in the Earth days between seasons, your natural season at work is the transition: handovers, reorganizations, new systems replacing old ones. You're steady when others feel unsettled. Volunteer for transition projects. You're better at them than most people.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Earth-days born: volunteer for the transition projects. You shine there.

output.heading: What goes missing when you burn out
output.text: Your chart is short on its output element, so when you burn out, expression goes first. You stop sharing ideas, stop joking, stop telling anyone how you feel. Colleagues may not notice until it's serious. Tell one person early: 'I'm running low.' Saying it is the output your chart is missing.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: 'I'm running low.' Say it to one person, early.

wealth.heading: What goes missing when you burn out
wealth.text: Your chart is short on its wealth element, so when you burn out, motivation for results goes first. You still do the work, but you stop caring where it leads. Reconnect with one small goal you actually want, even if it's tiny. Purpose is the fastest fuel for you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Find one tiny goal you actually want. Purpose refuels you fastest.

power.heading: What goes missing when you burn out
power.text: Your chart is short on its power element, so when you burn out, structure goes first. Your days dissolve, tasks pile up unsorted, and everything feels equally urgent. Rebuild the frame: fixed hours, a short daily list, one thing finished before noon.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rebuild the frame: fixed hours and one thing done before noon.

resource.heading: What goes missing when you burn out
resource.text: Your chart is short on its resource element, so when you burn out, support goes first, or rather, you stop accepting it. You isolate and push through alone. Let someone help with something specific. Being supported is the missing piece, and you're allowed to have it.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Let someone help with one specific thing. You're allowed.

none.heading: What goes missing when you burn out
none.text: All five elements show up in your chart, so burnout doesn't have one obvious entry point for you. It creeps in through whichever part of life you've neglected longest. Check the basics regularly: sleep, people, movement, meaning. The one you've been skipping is your door.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Check the basics weekly. Burnout enters where you stopped looking.

yang.heading: Your work rhythm: yang
yang.text: Your Day Master is yang, the outward half of saju's pair. At work that means you push forward in visible bursts: big efforts, public commitments, decisive moves. You recover by changing scene. When you're stuck, go outside, switch projects, or talk it through with someone. Movement unsticks you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Yang rhythm: stuck? Change the scene. Movement unsticks you.

yin.heading: Your work rhythm: yin
yin.text: Your Day Master is yin, the inward half of saju's pair. At work that means steady, thoughtful progress, often invisible until it's finished. You recover by going inward. When you're stuck, close the door, write it down, or sleep on it. Quiet unsticks you.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Yin rhythm: stuck? Close the door and sleep on it.

strong.heading: How your chart takes criticism
strong.text: A strong chart takes criticism with a straight back and sometimes a raised shield. You can handle it, but your first instinct is to defend. Give yourself one rule: in the meeting, only ask questions. Defend, if you still need to, the next day.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: In the meeting, only questions. Defend tomorrow, if still needed.

weak.heading: How your chart takes criticism
weak.text: A weak chart takes criticism into the body: a hot face, a sinking stomach, a night of replaying. That reaction is normal for you, not a sign the feedback was devastating. Write down the actual words that were said. They're usually much kinder than the version in your head.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your inner critic exaggerates. Check the real wording.

wood.heading: Your ideal workspace
wood.text: Your balancing element is Wood, so your ideal workspace has growth in it: plants, daylight, a view of trees if you're lucky, and a role with room to expand. Standing desks, walking meetings and a bookshelf of things you're learning all count.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood workspace: plants, daylight, walking meetings.

fire.heading: Your ideal workspace
fire.text: Your balancing element is Fire, so your ideal workspace is bright and alive: good light, energetic people, a place where your work is seen. Open spaces suit you better than isolated offices, as long as you can escape for a quiet hour.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire workspace: bright, buzzing, with one escape room.

earth.heading: Your ideal workspace
earth.text: Your balancing element is Earth, so your ideal workspace is stable and comfortable: the same desk every day, good chairs, a kitchen with real food, and a team that sticks around. Hot desking and constant moves will drain you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth workspace: same desk, good chair, real food.

metal.heading: Your ideal workspace
metal.text: Your balancing element is Metal, so your ideal workspace is clean and ordered: a tidy desk, clear systems, good tools and little clutter, visual or procedural. Minimal setups help you think.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal workspace: tidy desk, good tools, zero clutter.

water.heading: Your ideal workspace
water.text: Your balancing element is Water, so your ideal workspace is flexible: remote days, a quiet corner, travel now and then, and freedom over when you work. Bonus points for anywhere near water.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water workspace: flexible hours, a quiet corner, maybe a view of water.

rat.heading: Your Friday ritual
rat.text: With the Rat under you, end the week by tying up loose threads: three quick replies you've been avoiding, then out the door.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rat Friday: three avoided replies, then out the door.

ox.heading: Your Friday ritual
ox.text: With the Ox under you, end the week with your tidy-desk routine and the same comforting dinner every Friday.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ox Friday: tidy desk, favorite dinner. Ritual complete.

tiger.heading: Your Friday ritual
tiger.text: With the Tiger under you, end the week with something physical and a little bold: a hike, a climbing gym, a spontaneous trip.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Tiger Friday: something physical and slightly reckless.

rabbit.heading: Your Friday ritual
rabbit.text: With the Rabbit under you, end the week somewhere pretty with someone gentle: a café, a gallery, a good friend.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rabbit Friday: somewhere pretty, someone gentle.

dragon.heading: Your Friday ritual
dragon.text: With the Dragon under you, end the week by writing down next week's big idea, then celebrating like it already worked.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Dragon Friday: write the big idea, celebrate early.

snake.heading: Your Friday ritual
snake.text: With the Snake under you, end the week quietly: a long bath, a thriller, nobody asking you anything.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Snake Friday: bath, thriller, nobody asking anything.

horse.heading: Your Friday ritual
horse.text: With the Horse under you, end the week moving: a run, a dance class, or a night out with the loudest friends you have.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Horse Friday: run, dance, loud friends.

goat.heading: Your Friday ritual
goat.text: With the Goat under you, end the week making something by hand: cooking, drawing, a small craft, anything that's not a screen.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Goat Friday: make something with your hands.

monkey.heading: Your Friday ritual
monkey.text: With the Monkey under you, end the week with a game, a puzzle or a new gadget to take apart.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Monkey Friday: a puzzle or a gadget to dismantle.

rooster.heading: Your Friday ritual
rooster.text: With the Rooster under you, end the week by planning a perfect Saturday and dressing nicely for no reason.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Rooster Friday: plan Saturday, dress up for nobody.

dog.heading: Your Friday ritual
dog.text: With the Dog under you, end the week with your oldest friends, the ones who knew you before this job.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Dog Friday: old friends, zero work talk.

pig.heading: Your Friday ritual
pig.text: With the Pig under you, end the week with a feast, a nap and absolutely no alarms set for Saturday.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Pig Friday: feast, nap, zero Saturday alarms.

spring.heading: Your best stretch of the year
spring.text: Spring-born, your work energy tends to peak when the days get longer: late winter into spring. That's the time for pitches, new roles and big conversations with your manager. In the heavy months of late autumn, lower the bar on yourself a little and focus on finishing rather than starting.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Spring-born: pitch when the days get longer.

summer.heading: Your best stretch of the year
summer.text: Summer-born, you tend to run strongest in the bright, busy months. Use that window for the projects that need the most energy and visibility. When winter comes, plan, learn and rest instead of forcing launches. Your fire comes back with the light.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Summer-born: launch in the light, plan in the dark months.

autumn.heading: Your best stretch of the year
autumn.text: Autumn-born, your sharpest months are usually the crisp ones, when the year turns toward results and deadlines. Schedule your hardest analytical work and your reviews then. Spring's chaos can feel scattered to you; use it for exploring rather than deciding.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Autumn-born: save the hard thinking for crisp months.

winter.heading: Your best stretch of the year
winter.text: Winter-born, you often think most clearly when the world slows down. The quiet weeks around the end of the year are gold for strategy, writing and deep work. Summer's social whirl drains you faster than others; protect a few quiet evenings even in July.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Winter-born: the quiet end of the year is your gold.

earth.heading: Your best stretch of the year
earth.text: Born in the Earth days, you do best in the in-between weeks, when one season or project hands over to the next. You're steady during change. Volunteer for planning the next phase while others are still finishing the last one.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Earth-days born: you shine in the handover weeks.

peer.heading: Your feedback habit
peer.text: Since {heavy_el} turns up most in your chart, you give feedback as an equal: direct, frank, a little competitive. It works well with peers and can land too hard on juniors. With anyone junior, add one sentence on how you'd help them fix it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Peer-to-peer frankness. Add a helping sentence for juniors.

output.heading: Your feedback habit
output.text: Since {heavy_el} turns up most in your chart, your feedback is vivid and creative, full of ideas for how it could be better. Sometimes so full that the person drowns. Pick your favorite idea and hold the rest for another day.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Your feedback overflows with ideas. Choose the best one.

wealth.heading: Your feedback habit
wealth.text: Since {heavy_el} turns up most in your chart, your feedback is practical and results-focused: what needs to change to hit the goal. Clear and useful. Add one line about the person's effort, not only their output.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Results-focused feedback. Mention the effort too.

power.heading: Your feedback habit
power.text: Since {heavy_el} turns up most in your chart, your feedback is structured and fair, often referencing standards and rules. It's credible. It can also sound like a verdict. Turn one statement into a question: 'What would you change here?'

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Turn one verdict into a question. Watch them engage.

resource.heading: Your feedback habit
resource.text: Since {heavy_el} turns up most in your chart, your feedback is thoughtful and explanatory, almost a lesson. People learn a lot. They also sometimes miss the bottom line. Say the main point first, then teach.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Main point first, then the lesson.

output.heading: The skill worth borrowing
output.text: With no {miss_el} in your visible pillars, the work skill worth borrowing is self-presentation: talking about your work, demos, writing up what you did. It won't come naturally. It's learnable, like a language. Practice on low-stakes updates first.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Borrow self-presentation. Practice on small updates first.

wealth.heading: The skill worth borrowing
wealth.text: With no {miss_el} in your visible pillars, the skill worth borrowing is negotiation: asking for resources, scope and recognition. Read one good book on it, then practice asking for one small thing a month.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Negotiation is a learnable skill. Start tiny, start this month.

power.heading: The skill worth borrowing
power.text: With no {miss_el} in your visible pillars, the skill worth borrowing is self-management: calendars, deadlines, systems that keep you on track when motivation dips. Tools are your friends here. Pick one system and stick with it for three months.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Borrow self-management. One system, three months.

resource.heading: The skill worth borrowing
resource.text: With no {miss_el} in your visible pillars, the skill worth borrowing is learning on purpose: courses, mentors, reading. You tend to learn by doing, which is fast but patchy. Fill the gaps deliberately.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Borrow learning on purpose. Fill the gaps doing leaves.

none.heading: The skill worth borrowing
none.text: With all five elements present, you don't have one glaring gap. The skill worth borrowing is focus: choosing what not to do. Range is a gift until it scatters you. Write a short 'not doing this year' list.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Write a 'not doing this year' list. Range needs edges.

gap-wood.text:
In a meeting, Gap Wood sits up straight and speaks early, usually to set direction: 'So what are we actually trying to decide?' People are grateful, because the meeting suddenly has a spine. You also defend whoever isn't in the room. If someone criticizes a colleague who's absent, you'll say 'let's ask them first.' That earns quiet loyalty.

Your meeting weakness is the second hour. Once the decision you cared about is made, you mentally leave and start planning next steps on your laptop. Others notice. Either keep meetings short enough for your attention, or give yourself a role for the end, like summarizing actions. Pines are good at standing tall at the start. Practice staying rooted until the last agenda item.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You give the meeting a spine. Stay rooted till the last item.

gap-wood.heading: You in a meeting

eul-wood.text:
In a meeting, Eul Wood reads the room before speaking. You track who's tense, who's bored and who's about to be steamrolled, and you wait for the moment your point will land softly. When you finally talk, it's often the compromise everyone suddenly agrees with. That's a real skill, and it rarely gets credited by name.

Your meeting weakness is waiting too long. Sometimes the right moment never comes and you leave with your idea unsaid, then mention it in the hallway, where it doesn't count. Try speaking in the first ten minutes at least once, even with a small question. It plants you in the conversation. Vines need a first anchor point before they can climb.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Speak once in the first ten minutes. Plant your anchor.

eul-wood.heading: You in a meeting

byeong-fire.text:
In a meeting, Byeong Fire is the energy source. You arrive with a story, crack the first joke, and push the group toward a bold option. On a dull Tuesday that's a gift. People leave your meetings more awake than they arrived.

Your meeting weakness is airtime. You can fill a whole meeting without meaning to, and quieter colleagues stop trying to compete with the sun. Set yourself a small rule: after you speak, ask someone specific what they think. 'Mina, you know this area better than me, what am I missing?' You'll still be the brightest person in the room. You'll also be the one who made everyone else visible, which is the more senior skill.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: After you speak, name someone and ask what they think.

byeong-fire.heading: You in a meeting

jeong-fire.text:
In a meeting, Jeong Fire is the one who asks the question that makes everyone pause. Not loud, not long, just precise: 'Who is this actually for?' You notice the human side of a plan, the customer who'll be confused, the colleague who'll get the extra work. That warmth makes your contributions memorable.

Your meeting weakness is taking the mood home. A tense discussion, a dismissive comment, a colleague's sigh: you'll replay it on the commute. Give yourself a short ritual after hard meetings, a walk to the coffee machine, two lines in a notebook about what was actually decided. The candle stays steady if the draft has somewhere to go.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: After a tense meeting: walk, then two lines on what was decided.

jeong-fire.heading: You in a meeting

mu-earth.text:
In a meeting, Mu Earth is the calm center. You don't say much in the first half. Then, when the group is going in circles, you summarize the situation in three sentences and suggest a way forward. People defer to you, partly because you sound so certain and partly because you usually are.

Your meeting weakness is the closed door. Once you've decided something is wrong, new arguments bounce off you, and colleagues stop trying. Leave one window open: 'What would change my mind here?' Say it aloud. Mountains are trusted for being stable. They're loved when they also turn out to be listening.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Leave one window open. Let a new argument in.

mu-earth.heading: You in a meeting

gi-earth.text:
In a meeting, Gi Earth is the one who brought the snacks, took the notes and remembered the action item from last month. You make meetings work. You also notice who hasn't spoken and gently bring them in. Teams with you in them feel more like teams.

Your meeting weakness is volunteering. Every time a task floats in the air without an owner, your hand goes up. By Friday you're doing four people's follow-ups. Try counting to five before you volunteer. Often someone else picks it up in that pause, and if nobody does, you'll know it truly needs you. Gardens feed everyone. They still need a fence around the vegetable patch.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Count to five before you volunteer. Someone else often will.

gi-earth.heading: You in a meeting

gyeong-metal.text:
In a meeting, Gyeong Metal cuts. You spot the weak point in the plan within minutes and say it plainly. Decisions happen faster with you there, and projects avoid some expensive mistakes. Leaders love bringing you in to stress-test an idea.

Your meeting weakness is the angle of the blade. You can say the right thing in a way that makes the person who proposed the idea defensive for the rest of the hour. Try sandwiching it, not with fake praise, but with a real question: 'I like where this is going. What happens if the supplier is late?' Same point, and the person stays on your side. Swords are most useful when people are glad to see them.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Raise the weak point as a question. Same point, fewer enemies.

gyeong-metal.heading: You in a meeting

sin-metal.text:
In a meeting, Sin Metal is the quality check. You notice the typo on slide nine, the inconsistent number in the summary, the deadline that doesn't add up. Colleagues tease you for it and then quietly send you their decks before big presentations. Your standards make the whole team look better.

Your meeting weakness is staying silent on the big picture because you're polishing details. You often have a sharp view on strategy too, and you hold it back until you're sure. Share it at eighty percent. Jewels are judged on clarity, and a clear opinion offered a little early is worth more than a perfect one that arrives after the decision.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Share your big-picture view at eighty percent. Early beats perfect.

sin-metal.heading: You in a meeting

im-water.text:
In a meeting, Im Water connects things nobody else connected. 'This is the same problem the sales team had last year.' 'What if we combined these two projects?' You see systems, and your ideas often reshape the whole discussion. The best meetings for you are the open ones, brainstorming, strategy, anything with a whiteboard.

Your meeting weakness is drift. Status updates and detailed reviews bore you, and colleagues can see you've gone somewhere else. If you can't avoid them, give yourself a job: track the decisions, or spot links to other teams. Oceans stay interesting to themselves when they have a current to follow. Give your mind one, even in the dullest weekly sync.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Status updates bore you. A small job keeps your current moving.

im-water.heading: You in a meeting

gye-water.text:
In a meeting, Gye Water is the quiet observer who says the one thing everyone was feeling. 'I think we're all a bit worried about the timeline.' The room exhales. You sense undercurrents, unspoken tension, the person who disagrees but won't say so. That makes you an excellent facilitator, whatever your job title.

Your meeting weakness is self-doubt after speaking. You'll say something insightful, then spend the afternoon wondering if it sounded silly. It didn't. Write down one thing you contributed after each meeting, as evidence. Rain doesn't measure itself drop by drop. It just notices, a month later, that everything grew.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: After each meeting, write down one thing you added. Evidence.

gye-water.heading: You in a meeting

gap-wood.text:
In a job interview, Gap Wood comes across as solid and principled. You talk about teams you built and problems you owned, and interviewers can picture you leading. The question that trips you is 'What's your weakness?', because you hate looking anything less than upright. Have a true answer ready, like taking on too much responsibility, with one example of how you now delegate.

When choosing between offers, ask about growth paths explicitly: 'Where could this role be in two years?' A pine without room to grow taller turns into a very frustrated pine. The title matters less to you than the direction, so pick the job with the clearest upward line.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Pick the offer with the clearest upward line, not the shiniest title.

gap-wood.heading: You in an interview

eul-wood.text:
In a job interview, Eul Wood is likable within minutes. You mirror the interviewer's energy, find common ground and tell stories about collaboration. The risk is underselling. You'll say 'we did' when you mean 'I did,' and the interviewer can't tell what was yours. Practice three 'I' sentences before every interview and use all of them.

When choosing between offers, look at the people more than the package. Vines grow best on a good wall, and for you that's a team that's warm, flexible and open to new ideas. Ask to meet one future teammate before signing. Ten minutes over coffee will tell you more than the job description ever could.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Practice three 'I did' sentences before every interview.

eul-wood.heading: You in an interview

byeong-fire.text:
In a job interview, Byeong Fire lights the room. You're enthusiastic, articulate and memorable, and interviewers often walk out smiling. The trap is overpromising. Excited in the moment, you agree to responsibilities you'd never choose on a calm day. Before you say yes to a new scope, ask for a day to think.

When choosing between offers, choose visibility. You do your best work where people see it: client-facing roles, teams with real launches, companies proud of what they make. A brilliant role hidden in a back office will dim you faster than you expect. Ask how success is recognized there, and listen closely to the answer.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ask how success gets recognized there. You need to be seen.

byeong-fire.heading: You in an interview

jeong-fire.text:
In a job interview, Jeong Fire is thoughtful and sincere. You don't oversell. You speak carefully about the work you care about, and interviewers sense the depth. The challenge is nerves: you can feel the interviewer's mood and adjust too much, getting smaller if they seem cold. Pick one story you're proud of and tell it fully, whatever their face is doing.

When choosing between offers, choose meaning and a decent manager. A candle needs shelter, and your boss is the shelter. Ask how they give feedback and what happens when someone makes a mistake. The answer predicts your daily life better than the salary range.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Their answer about mistakes predicts your Tuesdays.

jeong-fire.heading: You in an interview

mu-earth.text:
In a job interview, Mu Earth comes across as reliable and grounded. You answer clearly, don't rush, and seem like someone who'll still be there in five years. Interviewers trust you. The risk is seeming too steady, as if you lack ambition. Mention one thing you want to build, in concrete terms, so they see the drive under the calm.

When choosing between offers, look at stability and scope. Mountains do best in organizations that won't reorganize every six months and that let you own something real. Ask how long people on the team have been there. A team with long tenure usually means leadership that keeps its word, and that's your kind of ground.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Ask how long the team has stayed. Long tenure is your ground.

mu-earth.heading: You in an interview

gi-earth.text:
In a job interview, Gi Earth is warm, prepared and easy to like. You researched the company, remembered the interviewer's name and asked about their weekend. The risk is shrinking your own achievements to seem humble. Bring numbers. 'I organized onboarding for forty new hires' sounds as big as it was.

When choosing between offers, choose a culture that values care and gives it back. Ask how the team supports people during busy seasons. If the answer is vague, picture yourself becoming everyone's unpaid helper there. Gardens thrive when somebody also waters them, so pick the place that has a watering plan.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Bring numbers to interviews. Humble shouldn't mean invisible.

gi-earth.heading: You in an interview

gyeong-metal.text:
In a job interview, Gyeong Metal is direct and decisive. You answer the question asked, give real examples and don't pad. Many interviewers love it. Some find it intimidating. Add one moment of warmth: a story about a colleague you helped, or a laugh about a project that went sideways. It shows the person behind the edge.

When choosing between offers, choose clarity. Clear goals, clear authority, clear consequences. A job with fuzzy responsibilities will frustrate you within months. Ask: 'Who decides when we disagree?' If nobody can answer, that's a role where your sword will spend its days cutting fog.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Fuzzy authority frustrates you fast. Check who makes the call.

gyeong-metal.heading: You in an interview

sin-metal.text:
In a job interview, Sin Metal is polished: good outfit, good portfolio, crisp answers. You make a strong first impression. Underneath, you're grading every word you say, which can make you seem a bit guarded. Let one answer be imperfect and personal, like what you love about your field. It makes the polish feel human.

When choosing between offers, choose quality. Companies that care about craft, detail and standards will make you happy. A place that ships sloppy work will drain you even if it pays well. Ask to see something the team made recently. Your reaction in the first five seconds will tell you whether you belong there.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Ask to see their recent work. Your first reaction is the answer.

sin-metal.heading: You in an interview

im-water.text:
In a job interview, Im Water is curious and expansive. You ask good questions, connect the role to bigger trends and sometimes end up interviewing them. That's impressive. It can also drift. Prepare two crisp examples with clear results, so your big ideas have proof attached.

When choosing between offers, choose freedom and range. Oceans need room: flexible hours, varied projects, permission to explore. A narrow role with strict processes will feel like being kept in a tank. Ask what a typical week looks like. If every week sounds the same, keep looking, or negotiate for a side project from the start.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: If every week sounds identical, that role is a fish tank.

im-water.heading: You in an interview

gye-water.text:
In a job interview, Gye Water is perceptive and gentle. You pick up what the interviewer really cares about and speak to it, sometimes without them realizing. The risk is nerves turning into vagueness. Write your three key points on a card and glance at it before you go in. Clear rain is more useful than mist.

When choosing between offers, choose kindness and quiet. You do your deepest work in calm environments with emotionally intelligent people. Notice how the receptionist was treated, how the interviewer talked about their team, whether anyone laughed in the hallway. Your intuition about a place is usually right, so trust it more than the brochure.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Trust your read of the hallway. Your intuition is usually right.

gye-water.heading: You in an interview

strong.heading: You and your boss
strong.text:
A strong chart doesn't love being managed. You respect bosses who are competent and fair, and you quietly test the ones who aren't. If you think a decision is wrong, you'll say so, sometimes in front of others. That can earn respect or start a cold war, depending on the boss.

The smarter move is private disagreement and public support. Raise your objection one-on-one, with a better alternative. If the decision stands, back it in front of the team. Bosses remember who made them look good under pressure, and your autonomy grows faster when they trust you won't undercut them. Strong charts often end up leading. Practice being the kind of report you'd want to have.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Disagree in private, support in public. Autonomy grows faster.

weak.heading: You and your boss
weak.text:
A weak chart takes a boss's mood personally. A short email, a skipped one-on-one, a distracted face in a meeting, and you're wondering what you did wrong. Most of the time, nothing. Bosses are busy and grumpy for their own reasons.

Protect yourself with structure. Ask for a regular one-on-one, even fifteen minutes every two weeks, and bring a short list: what you did, what's blocking you, one question. It turns vague anxiety into a clear conversation. And ask directly once a quarter: 'Is there anything you'd like me to do differently?' Hearing the answer, usually small, is far better than imagining it.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fifteen minutes every two weeks with a short list. Anxiety shrinks.

wood.heading: Your way back
wood.text: Wood is the element that rebalances you, so getting back from a hard stretch begins with something growing. Not another goal at work. Something small and alive: a new route on your walk, a beginner's class in anything, a plant on the windowsill you actually water. Wood heals through forward motion, so even a tiny sense of progress outside work rebuilds what the job drained. Give it three weeks before you judge whether it's working.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Recover with something small that grows. Three weeks, then judge.

fire.heading: Your way back
fire.text: Fire is the element that rebalances you, so getting back from a hard stretch begins with warmth and people. Burnout tells you to hide. Do the opposite, gently: one dinner with a friend who makes you laugh, a concert, a sunny afternoon outdoors. Fire comes back through connection and light, not through lying in a dark room scrolling. One warm evening a week is a real treatment for your chart, not a luxury.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Burnout says hide. Book one warm evening with a funny friend.

earth.heading: Your way back
earth.text: Earth is the element that rebalances you, so getting back from a hard stretch begins with routine and the body's basics. Regular meals, the same bedtime, a walk at the same hour. It sounds boring because it is, and boring is what your system needs after chaos. Earth heals through predictability. Cook something simple on Sunday for the week ahead. Small, steady structure gives your mind solid ground to stand on again.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Same bedtime, same walk, simple Sunday cooking. Boring heals you.

metal.heading: Your way back
metal.text: Metal is the element that rebalances you, so getting back from a hard stretch begins with cutting things out. Unsubscribe, decline, delete the app, clear the desk. Burnout for you is usually too many open loops. Make a list of every commitment, then cross off three you can drop or delay. Metal heals through clarity. The relief of an emptier calendar will do more for you than any spa weekend.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: List every commitment. Cross off three. Clarity heals you.

water.heading: Your way back
water.text: Water is the element that rebalances you, so getting back from a hard stretch begins with stillness and sleep. Real rest, not productive rest. A morning with no plans, a long bath, an evening of reading something that has nothing to do with work. Water heals by settling, the way a muddy glass clears when you stop shaking it. Give your mind a few unstructured hours each week and let the sediment sink.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Stop shaking the glass. Unstructured hours let the mud settle.

wood.heading: Your email style
wood.text: Wood writes emails that point somewhere. Subject line with a verb, a clear ask, a next step and a date. Colleagues like knowing what you want. The habit to watch is the long 'one more thing' paragraph at the end, where three new projects quietly sneak in. Send those as separate emails, later. One email, one direction, is the Wood rule that keeps people actually reading you.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Wood email rule: one email, one direction. Extras go later.

fire.heading: Your email style
fire.text: Fire writes warm emails: exclamation marks, thanks, a friendly line about the weekend. People enjoy hearing from you. The risk is that the actual request gets buried under the warmth, and nobody acts on it. Put the ask in the first two lines, then be as lovely as you like. And never answer an email that made you angry within the hour. Fire types send the reply they regret fastest.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Fire email rule: the ask in line one. Angry replies wait an hour.

earth.heading: Your email style
earth.text: Earth writes reliable emails. You reply, you confirm, you follow up when others forget. Your inbox is a small act of care for the whole team. The habit to watch is over-explaining: three paragraphs of context before the point, in case anyone feels left out. Try bullet points and a short summary up top. Steady and short reads as confident, not cold.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Earth email rule: summary on top, bullets below. Short reads confident.

metal.heading: Your email style
metal.text: Metal writes short emails. Sometimes very short. 'Fine.' 'No.' 'See attached.' Efficient, and occasionally terrifying for the person on the other end, who reads it three times looking for anger that isn't there. Add one human line. 'Thanks for the quick turnaround' costs four seconds and saves a colleague a worried afternoon. Precise doesn't have to mean frosty.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Metal email rule: add one human line. Four seconds, much kinder.

water.heading: Your email style
water.text: Water writes thoughtful emails, sometimes so thoughtful they arrive three days late. You want to answer properly, so you wait until you have time, and then the thread has moved on. Try a quick holding reply: 'Got it, full answer by Thursday.' It keeps the current moving. Your deep replies are worth waiting for; people just need to know they're coming.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Water email rule: a quick 'got it, more by Thursday' keeps things flowing.

mu-earth.how-you-work:
Mu Earth works like a mountain: steady, reliable and very hard to move once you've settled on a plan. You're the colleague everyone trusts with the critical stuff, the year-end close, the client who's about to leave, the system that can't go down. You don't panic. You show up, you do the work, and you keep doing it.

You work best with stability and clear responsibilities. Constant reorganizations and shifting priorities make you grumpy, because you like building something solid and then maintaining it properly. You're patient with long projects and excellent at holding the details of complex operations in your head.

The habit to watch is resistance to change. You can dismiss new ideas because the current way works. Sometimes it does. Ask yourself, when you feel the 'no' coming, whether you're protecting quality or protecting comfort.
mu-earth.how-you-lead:
Mu Earth leads by stability. Your team knows exactly what you expect, that you'll back them, and that you won't panic when things go wrong. People feel safe under you, and safe teams take smart risks.

Your style is calm, consistent and protective, and you may be slow to adapt. You'll defend an old process long after it should've been retired, and you can miss the early signs of a team member who's unhappy because they don't complain loudly.

The upgrade is regular, deliberate change: once a quarter, let the team pick one thing about how you work to experiment with. Mountains don't move, but the paths across them can be redrawn. It keeps your stability from turning into stagnation.
mu-earth.coworkers:
On a team, Mu Earth is the rock. People come to you for help, for calm, for a straight answer. You're loyal to colleagues who've earned it and generous with your time.

You clash with fast, chaotic colleagues who change plans constantly, cut corners and expect you to scramble. Your response is to get more fixed, which they read as stubbornness. You also clash with people who try to rush you into decisions. Name your timeline: 'I'll have an answer for you Thursday.' It gives the fast people certainty, and it gives you the time you need.
mu-earth.burnout:
Mu Earth burns out by holding too much weight for too long. Mountains don't complain, and neither do you. You'll carry a team, a crisis and a difficult manager for a year without a word, and then find you've lost all motivation and gained a permanent ache in your shoulders.

Your warning signs: everything feeling heavy, withdrawing from colleagues, and a flat 'whatever' where you used to care. Recovery means putting things down: delegate, say no to new responsibilities, and spend time somewhere that holds you instead, a home that feels safe, good food, nature, routines that don't require effort.
mu-earth.job-vibe:
Stable, responsible and foundational: that's the job vibe for Mu Earth, the kind of work where reliability matters more than flash. Operations, finance, project management, engineering, logistics, real estate, public service, healthcare administration, law, anything where people depend on things working.

You struggle in chaotic startups that pivot every month and in roles that reward hype over substance. You need solid ground and a clear role, and you'll hold it longer than anyone.

mu-earth.speaker: bom
mu-earth.text: The mountain at work: steady, and very hard to move.

mu-earth.speaker: yeon
mu-earth.text: The 'no' is coming. Quality or comfort? Ask yourself.

mu-earth.speaker: bom
mu-earth.text: Your team takes smart risks because you're calm.

mu-earth.speaker: yeon
mu-earth.text: Old process, new decade. Maybe retire it.

mu-earth.speaker: bom
mu-earth.text: 'Thursday.' One word, and the fast people relax.

mu-earth.speaker: yeon
mu-earth.text: Mountains don't complain. That's the problem.

spring.intro:
Earth born in spring is a field full of roots pushing up through it, everything wanting something from the soil. The season tests you: the season you were born in presses on your element. At work that gave you discipline and a strong sense of responsibility early. You respect structure, meet deadlines and handle authority well. You can also be hard on yourself and slow to ask for help. A boss who praises as well as corrects brings out your best.

For Mu Earth at work, this season shapes the mountain you become: a peak people climb to see far, or a broad slope that quietly holds a whole valley.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Disciplined since forever. You deserve a boss who praises too.

summer.intro:
Summer Earth is ground baked warm by the sun, dry, solid and holding the heat long after dark. The season feeds you: your birth season feeds your element. At work that looks like someone who learns quickly and benefits enormously from good mentors, training and support. You absorb a workplace's knowledge like soil absorbs rain. Choose jobs where people will teach you, because you turn teaching into skill faster than most.

For Mu Earth at work, this season shapes the mountain you become: a peak people climb to see far, or a broad slope that quietly holds a whole valley.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: Pick jobs with great teachers. You learn faster than anyone.

earth.intro:
Earth born in the Earth days is a mountain standing on more mountain, about as solid as saju gets. Element match: your birth season carries your own element, so at work you start out sure of how you like to operate. You have a strong default style and you settle into a new job fast. The flip side is friction with workplaces that run on a very different rhythm. You'd rather change jobs than change your whole way of working, and sometimes that's exactly right.

For Mu Earth at work, this season shapes the mountain you become: a peak people climb to see far, or a broad slope that quietly holds a whole valley.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: Strong default style. Sometimes the job has to fit you.

autumn.intro:
Earth born in autumn is the field at harvest, giving up its gold one cart at a time. You pour into the season: your birth season draws your element outward. At work that makes you a doer and a maker: you need to produce something visible, a project, a design, a result you can point to. Jobs that are all meetings and no output leave you restless. The risk is overproducing and running yourself down, so build in recovery the way you build in deadlines.

For Mu Earth at work, this season shapes the mountain you become: a peak people climb to see far, or a broad slope that quietly holds a whole valley.

panel.speaker: bom
panel.text: You need to make something visible. Meetings alone won't do it.

winter.intro:
Earth born in winter is frozen ground by a cold river, firm on top and full of water underneath. You shape the season: your element works on the season you were born in. At work that's a results person: you like targets, tangible progress and the satisfaction of managing resources well. You're good at turning messy situations into organized ones. Watch for treating every week like a quarter-end close. Not everything needs optimizing.

For Mu Earth at work, this season shapes the mountain you become: a peak people climb to see far, or a broad slope that quietly holds a whole valley.

panel.speaker: yeon
panel.text: You'd optimize your lunch break. Not everything needs a plan.

mu-earth.strong:
Your chart is strong, which at work means drive, confidence and a natural pull toward running things. You trust your own judgment, you recover from setbacks fast, and you don't need much external motivation. The blind spot is pushing: overruling colleagues, taking over projects that weren't yours, and assuming your pace is everyone's pace. Your best work years come when that drive is aimed at a clear goal and shared with a team you trust.

Mu Earth with this much support is immovable in meetings. Make sure it's principle, not habit.
mu-earth.weak:
Your chart is the weak kind, which at work means sensitivity, adaptability and a gift for reading what a team needs. You're often the colleague who makes collaboration work. The blind spot is giving too much: saying yes to every request, doubting your own ideas, letting louder people take credit. Your best work years come when you're in an environment that supports you and when you protect your energy as carefully as your output.

Mu Earth on a lighter chart carries less weight easily. Don't let people pile on more than you'd choose.

feedback.text:
Mu Earth hears feedback out without reacting and then changes nothing, unless the case is convincing. You need evidence, not opinions. Feedback that comes with examples and a clear reason earns a real change from you. Feedback based on feelings bounces off.

Giving feedback, you're straightforward and fair but can be heavy. You list what's wrong like a report, and people feel flattened. Lighten it. Pick the one most important point, explain why it matters, and offer your help fixing it. One point delivered well changes more than five delivered thoroughly.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Show you evidence and you'll change. Feelings bounce off.

panels.speaker: yeon
panels.text: One point, delivered well. Not a five-page report.

best-week.text: Mu Earth's best week at work: Monday, the plan is clear and nothing changes it. Tuesday to Thursday, steady progress on something important, with time to do it properly. A colleague comes to you with a problem and leaves calmer. Friday, everything you're responsible for is in order, nobody is panicking, and you go home to a good meal and a quiet weekend. Stability, a job done right, one person helped, and a real rest. Fight for weeks like this, they're not boring, they're how mountains stay standing.

panels.speaker: bom
panels.text: Nothing on fire, everything in order, a good meal Friday night.

job-list.heading: Roles in that vibe
job-list.text: Roles that suit the mountain: operations manager, controller, project director, civil engineer, logistics lead, property manager, public sector specialist, the person who keeps the critical system running. The thread is responsibility and something solid to protect.
